subject: Private inference access mode heatmap: peering vs interface endpoints vs S2S VPN

- Latency-to-inference should be as low as possible (target p50 < 50ms from our API layer in us-west-2).
- No public internet egress for model data (all traffic must be over private links).

Alex — thanks for the context and diagram. High-level recommendations up front, with trade-offs and a simple "heatmap" view attached (access-mode-heatmap.xlsx):

1) VPC peering (direct peering between your VPC and Redwood's hosting VPC)
   - Pros: Lowest additional network hop/latency, straightforward routing for single-account setups.
   - Cons: Scales poorly for many customer VPCs (routing table limits), requires non-overlapping IP ranges, limited cross-region utility; operational blast radius if misconfigured.

2) Provider interface endpoints / PrivateLink (Redwood exposes interface endpoints into your VPC)
   - Pros: Strong security posture (no route propagation), fine-grained control, multi-account friendly, easiest for audited isolation.
   - Cons: Slightly higher per-request cost on some clouds, introduces ENI/endpoint quotas, and traffic path can add a few ms compared to peering depending on cloud internals.

3) Site-to-site VPN
   - Pros: Works well for on-prem or legacy network connectivity, simple to set up for low throughput, keeps traffic off the public internet with IPSec tunnels.
   - Cons: Higher latency and jitter, MTU/path-MTU issues for high throughput; not ideal as primary low-latency path unless you layer with a private link.

Given your p50 <50ms target and no public egress requirement, my short recommendation: Primary = Provider interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for security/auditability and supportability; Secondary = S2S VPN for on-prem clusters or as a resilient fallback if PrivateLink suffers an outage. VPC peering is attractive only if you have a single VPC and allocated non-overlapping CIDRs and want the absolute lowest tail latency.

I've attached an XLS heatmap that scores each option versus your constraints and operational burden. Next: Karthik can outline the specific IP/routing and MTU considerations and whether we should propose a Transit Gateway design if you expect many spoke VPCs.

Jonas Weber
Director, Customer Solutions — Redwood Inference

Quick technical addendum from the runtime side:

- IP planning: We need a guaranteed /24 (or larger) of non-overlapping CIDR space on your side for any peering/transit route propagation. If you cannot provide that, PrivateLink avoids the overlap problem.
- MTU: If you expect large payloads (model context blobs, checkpoints), ensure path MTU >= 1400; VPNs often impose lower MTU and require fragmentation tuning.
- Throughput: VPN appliances on-prem or cloud-managed VPNs may throttle sustained token streams; for high QPS inference, test a canary first.
- NAT & SNAT: PrivateLink preserves source addressing in many clouds (useful for IP-based allowlists), peering definitely preserves it; VPN often requires SNAT depending on your edge.
- Transit gateway note: If you plan to connect many spoke VPCs or multiple on-prem sites, a Transit Gateway / Transit Backbone is reasonable; it increases cost but centralizes routing and ACLs.

If you want, we can run a 24–48 hour latency/throughput canary between a PrivateLink endpoint and a peered VPC in us-west-2 to measure delta; that will give concrete p50/p95 numbers for your traffic profile.

—Karthik
Principal Solutions Architect — Redwood Inference

Alex — sounds good, thanks. Actionable plan and decision notes:

Decision: Recommend PrivateLink (provider interface endpoints) as the primary connectivity mode, with an encrypted site-to-site VPN as a documented fallback/resilience path for your on-prem clusters. We will not pursue VPC peering given your IP overlap constraints.

Why: PrivateLink meets your audit/no-egress requirement, minimizes operational blast radius across multi-account setups, and avoids CIDR renumbering. The small latency delta is usually 2–8ms p50 in us-west-2 for control-plane and token streams; we will validate with the proposed canary.
